title: Impacts of Aggregation on Model Diversity and Consumer Utility
claim: Aggregated set value can decrease even as an individual element's value increases, revealing a non-monotone region under soft aggregation.
layout: 1 panel, single line plot, shaded region highlighting non-monotone zone
description: A single matplotlib line plot titled 'Value of set {v1, v2}'. The x-axis is v2, running from 0 to 5. The y-axis is the set value, running from 3.7 to 4.3 and above. A steel-blue curve starts near 3.93 at v2=0 and falls smoothly to a minimum of about 3.72 near v2≈2.7. It then rises steeply, crossing 4.0 at v2=4 and continuing above 4.3 by v2≈4.6. A dark red vertical line at v2=4 is labeled 'v1', marking the fixed value of the other element. The region from v2=0 to about 2.7 is shaded light pink and labeled 'Non-monotone region' in dark red text. The eye goes first to the blue curve's dip inside the shaded zone.
caption: Example demonstrating non-monotonicity (Definition [ref]) and non-monotonic region (Definition [ref]). Blue curve shows the value of a set containing two elements $\{v_1, v_2\}$, where aggregation is done with softmax with temperature $\beta$. $v_1$ has fixed value 4, while $v_2$'s value varies. Note that for parts of the figure, the value of $v_2$ increases, but the value of the set decreases.
abstract: Consider a marketplace of AI tools, each with slightly different strengths and weaknesses. By picking the right model for the task at hand, a user can do better than simply using the same model for everything. Routers operate under a similar principle, where sophisticated model selection can increase overall performance. However, aggregation is often noisy, reflecting imperfect user choices or routing decisions. This leads to two main questions: first, what does a "healthy marketplace" of models look like for maximizing consumer utility? Secondly, how can we incentivize producers to create such models? We show that winrate, a standard benchmark in LLM evaluation, can incentivize model creators to homogenize for both types of model changes, reducing consumer welfare. We propose a new mechanism, weighted winrate, which rewards models for answers that are higher quality, and show that it provably improves incentives for producers to specialize and increases consumer welfare. We conclude by exploring the impact of our theoretical results in empirical benchmark datasets and discussing implications for benchmark design.
